sections.body:
A **snack** is a small amount of food you eat between meals. It is not a meal. A meal is big enough to fill you up for hours. A snack is just enough to hold you until the next meal.

Snacks matter more than you might think. Your body is always working. It needs fuel at school, at play, and at homework. A good snack gives you that fuel.

But not all snacks are the same. Some snacks fill you up for a long time. Some fill you up for a short time and leave you hungry again. Some snacks are full of sugar. They taste great for a moment, and then you feel tired.

The rule is simple. A good snack has **three parts**. First, something to **chew**. Bread, carrots, apples, nuts or a boiled egg. Second, something **yellow**. Cheese, milk or yoghurt, because it has calcium. Third, something **sweet**. A piece of fruit, because fruit has natural sugar and vitamins.

Put the three parts on one plate, and you have a snack that will do your body good. Put only sweets on the plate, and you have a treat. Both are fine. Just know which one you are having.
examples: A snack is a small food between meals.
My snack has an apple, some cheese and a few crackers.
This is a treat, not a snack.
sections.heading: What a snack is

sections.body:
Some snacks keep you full until lunch. Others let you down ten minutes later. Here is how to tell them apart.

A snack with **fibre** keeps you full. Fibre is the part of food your body cannot digest. It sits in your tummy and makes you feel full. Fruit, vegetables, whole grains and nuts are all full of fibre.

A snack with **protein** keeps you full too. Protein is the building material of your body. It helps you grow and keeps your tummy happy. Eggs, cheese, milk, yoghurt, meat, beans and nuts all have protein.

A snack made only of **sugar** does not keep you full. Your body uses the sugar quickly. Then you feel hungry again, and your mood goes down. This is why a big bag of sweets never feels like enough.

Fats are slow fuel. A small handful of nuts has good fats, and they stay with you for hours. Just do not eat the whole bag.

Watch out for **hidden sugar**, too. It hides in drinks and in things you think are savoury. Some fizzy drinks have as much sugar as three or four sweets.

A good test: after your snack, are you still full at lunchtime? If yes, your snack was good.
examples: Apples have fibre, so they fill me up.
Nuts give me slow energy for a long time.
This fizzy drink has a lot of sugar in it.
sections.heading: Snacks that fill you up and snacks that do not

sections.body:
Here is a list of snacks that children all over the world eat. Some are easy, and some need a grown-up to help.

Fruit with yoghurt. Cut fruit into pieces and spoon it over yoghurt. It is sweet without sugar.

Crackers with cheese and tomato. Cut the tomato, put the cheese on top. It has protein, calcium and something to chew.

A boiled egg with bread. A boiled egg is quick and full of protein. It is a great after-school snack.

Oatcakes with nut butter. Spread the nut butter thin. Ask a grown-up if you are not sure about nuts.

Rice paper rolls. Fill them with vegetables and prawn or tofu. These are a Vietnamese favourite.

Popcorn. Plain popcorn is a whole grain and very filling. Ask for it without butter and salt.

Fruit and nut mix. A small handful is a good snack to carry.

Chickpeas, roasted. They are crunchy, full of protein, and fun to eat.

And of course, sometimes you want a biscuit or a piece of chocolate. Have it with a meal instead of on its own. Then it is a treat, and you enjoy it more.
examples: Today my snack was apple slices with yoghurt.
I made rice paper rolls with prawn.
I only had a small handful of nuts.
sections.heading: Snacks you can try this week

sections.body:
These are the words you will hear about food at school and at home.

A **snack** is a small amount of food between two meals.

A **treat** is something sweet you eat for fun. It is lovely, but it does not fill you up.

Fibre is the part of food your body cannot digest. It helps your tummy and keeps you full.

Protein is the building material of your body. It is in eggs, meat, beans, nuts, milk and cheese.

Sugar is a sweet food. Your body uses it for quick energy. Fruit has sugar inside it already.

A **balanced** snack has more than one kind of food, so you get more than one kind of goodness from it.
examples: A snack is food between two meals.
A treat is for fun, and a snack is for filling up.
sections.heading: The snack words, one by one

terms.example: I brought a snack to school for break time.
terms.gloss: A small amount of food that you eat between two meals.

terms.example: We have cake as a treat on Sunday.
terms.gloss: A sweet food you eat for fun, not to fill your tummy.

terms.example: Wholemeal bread has more fibre than white bread.
terms.gloss: The part of food your body cannot digest. It helps your tummy work and keeps you full.

terms.example: Eggs are full of protein, so they are a good snack.
terms.gloss: The building material of your body. It helps you grow and keeps you full for longer.

terms.example: A balanced snack has fruit, bread and cheese on it.
terms.gloss: Made of more than one kind of food, so you get more than one kind of goodness.

sections.body:
This is a way to build a snack that will do you good. It takes about two minutes. Ask a grown-up to help with sharp knives and nuts.

Look at your snack in three groups. Something to chew, something yellow, and something sweet. You can pick any food you like for each group. The plate does not have to be perfect.
examples: First I choose something to chew.
Last I add a piece of fruit.
sections.heading: How to build a snack plate
steps: Find something to chew: bread, a carrot, an apple or a boiled egg.
Find something yellow: cheese, milk or yoghurt.
Find something sweet: a piece of fruit.
Put all three on one plate or in one box.
Eat it slowly, sitting down, and enjoy it.

sections.body:
Sometimes you need to ask for a snack. Here is how to ask in a way that gets a yes.

Ask for the thing you want, and say why. "Can I have an apple after school? I am really hungry." is much better than "Can I have a snack?", which makes the grown-up do all the deciding.

If you are at school, ask your teacher. Say please, and say thank you when you get it.

You can also ask for what you do not want. "I am hungry, but I do not want the chips. Can I have fruit instead?" is a very strong sentence to know.

Some snacks are not safe for small children. Whole nuts and hard raw carrots can choke. Grate the carrot. Crush the nuts. And always sit down when you eat.

One more thing. Wash your hands before you eat, and keep your food away from anybody who is ill. If your snack has been on the table for hours, throw it away.

Now you know how to eat well and how to ask. That is a big grown-up skill.
examples: Can I have an apple after school? I am really hungry.
Can I have fruit instead of the chips, please?
I wash my hands before I eat my snack.
sections.heading: Asking for a snack and keeping it safe

item.summary: A snack is small food between meals. After reading this you can tell a snack from a meal, build a balanced snack plate, choose snacks that keep you full, and ask politely for one at school.
item.title: Healthy Snacks for Happy Kids
